subject: physics
question_text: Define Poisson’s ratio. What are its limiting values for steel?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 9 Very Short Answer Question 11 (printed p.98). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: σ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain is a dimensionless ratio of two strains, correctly unitless; the accepted range for steel, 0.27 to 0.30, matches the standard NCERT table of Poisson's ratios. BOOK TYPO (book p.98): the printed limits for steel read "027 - 0.30", a dropped decimal point — the correct value, 0.27 to 0.30, is written here instead.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Poisson’s ratio σ is the ratio of the
strain, for a rod under tension.
It is a pure number, with no unit.
steps.why: Both strains are produced by the same applied force, so their ratio is a single number that describes how much a material narrows as it stretches, independent of the actual size of the rod.
common_mistakes: Writing σ as longitudinal strain over lateral strain. The ratio is inverted; the lateral strain goes on top.
Giving σ a unit. Strain has no unit, so the ratio of two strains has none either.
steps.memory_tip: Lateral over longitudinal: the sideways strain sits on top of the ratio.
steps.margin_note: Marked for the words "lateral strain over longitudinal strain" — the bare formula alone does not earn it.

steps.label: Limits for steel
lines: For steel, Poisson’s ratio σ lies
steps.why: The limiting values are measured for real steel samples; they are quoted, not derived from a formula, so the numbers themselves are what the examiner is checking.
common_mistakes: Writing the limits as "027 to 0.30" with the decimal point dropped — the value is 0.27, not 27.
Quoting a value outside 0 to 0.5, which is impossible for an ordinary elastic solid.
steps.memory_tip: Steel sits low on the scale: 0.27 to 0.30, well under the 0.5 upper limit.
steps.margin_note: Marked for the two numbers, 0.27 and 0.30, in that order — write the decimal point clearly.

insider_note: Most answers lose the second mark by copying the book's dropped decimal point — write 0.27, never 027.
